criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban household drinking water supply conditions, continuity during weekly rationing, storage capacity, and per capita consumption among connected households in Campina Grande, Paraíba, Brazil.
criterion_notes.c2: PASSES PLAIN WORDING / FAILS NARROW 2026-10-13 READING. Under the plain literal wording of Criterion 2 ('Examines a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), the paper would pass because it studies a public utility's drought water-rationing management measure (CAGEPA's 36-hour weekly supply suspension) and describes federal-state water resource governance conflicts (ANA vs. Paraíba State/CAGEPA over Açude Boqueirão withdrawal permits) in the background section. Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type mechanism reading, however, Criterion 2 is NOT met: the ANA/state institutional narrative is unanalysed macro-governance background, and the empirical household analysis examines operational drought rationing interacted with socioeconomic status (household income/storage capacity) and engineering/topographic position in the pipe network ('hydraulic criterion': elevation and distance from system reservoirs). It does not empirically examine any rule-type mechanism governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, frontline discretion or accommodation, disconnection enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical data collected over 6 months (October 2014 to April 2015, covering 180 consecutive monitoring days from November 2014 to April 2015) via demographic/monitoring forms, direct household observation, and monthly semi-structured interviews across 17 stratified households.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports service availability/continuity and quantity outcomes at the household level, including monthly per capita water consumption (m3/month, Table 3), regular water storage capacity (liters, Table 2), relative water shortage hours over 180 days across hydraulic risk zones, and household water-use routine adaptations.
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and unit of analysis (17 urban households in Campina Grande stratified by income and hydraulic risk), empirical exposures (CAGEPA weekly drought rationing, household income, and hydraulic elevation/distance from reservoirs), outcomes (monthly per capita water consumption, storage capacity, shortage hours, and routine adaptations), and study design (6-month longitudinal qualitative/mixed-methods household monitoring study).
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English (with abstracts in English, Portuguese, and Spanish), which is directly eligible without translation.

evidence_quotes.quote: the current study about the water supply conditions in households and the perception of users about the impacts of water rationing on their water-use-related routines adopted two variables, namely: household income and risk of water shortage due to hydraulic criteria.
In early December 2014, the month that had followed the elections, CAGEPA started the water rationing in Campina Grande and in the other urban centers supplied by Açude Boqueirão.

The hydraulic criterion refers to the location of the households in relation to the reservoirs of the water supply system. The assumption is that the higher the topographic elevation of the households in relation to the reservoirs is and the greater the distance between the household and the reservoir, the greater the risk of water shortage.

The research underlying the current study was conducted by data collection on monthly visits that were carried out from October 2014 to April 2015. A non-random sample of households was stratified by the aforementioned variables.

In order to illustrate the herein performed analyses, Table 3 shows the households, according to household income and the average monthly per capita water consumption in the studied period, i.e., from November 2014 to April 2015.

Regarding the hydraulic criterion, data collected from the interviews with the householders located in the districts of Alto Branco, Cuités and Serrotão, which are areas of high water shortage risk, showed that those were who recorded the largest number of water shortage hours in a 180-day period, which started in November 1st 2014.

raw_response.exposure: Operational urban water rationing during drought (36-hour weekly supply suspension by utility CAGEPA from December 2014 to April 2015 vs. pre-rationing November 2014), stratified by household income and hydraulic shortage risk (topographic elevation and distance from supply reservoirs)
raw_response.outcome: Household water storage capacity (liters), average monthly per capita water consumption (m3/month), water shortage occurrences/hours over 180 days, and users' perceptions and adaptations in household water-use routines
raw_response.population_and_sample: Urban households connected to the CAGEPA water supply network in Campina Grande, Paraíba State, Brazil; non-random stratified sample of 17 households across four household income intervals and three hydraulic water-shortage risk levels (unit of analysis: household and resident interviewee)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure) under the 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism clarification to Criterion 2. Although the paper empirically monitors urban household water supply conditions, per capita consumption, storage capacity, and shortage hours across 17 households in Campina Grande, Brazil over 6 months (satisfying C1, C3, C4, C5, and C6), its empirical exposures are operational drought water rationing (a city-wide 36-hour weekly supply cutoff during reservoir scarcity) interacted with household income and physical/topographic hydraulic position in the distribution network. Its discussion of federal (ANA) versus state (CAGEPA/Paraíba) reservoir management is unanalysed macro-governance background, and no rule-type legal or administrative mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility rules, documentation/tenure requirements, administrative burden, tariff rules, discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or ownership/regulatory structure) is empirically examined. Under the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2, it would be included because utility drought rationing is a water management measure.
raw_response.study_design: Longitudinal qualitative and descriptive mixed-methods household monitoring study (6-month panel of monthly household visits, observation, and semi-structured interviews)
